cards.english: I am a student. (nominal sentence — no 'am')
cards.grammarNote:
Arabic has **no present-tense 'to be'**. Just place two words side by side:
**أنا طالب** (I [am a] student), **هي طبيبة** (she [is a] doctor), **الكتاب جديد** (the book [is] new).

**الـ** (al-) = 'the', attached to the front of the noun:
**كتاب** (a book) → **الكتاب** (the book). Before 'sun letters' (ت، س، ش، ن …) the **l** assimilates in sound: **الشمس** is said 'ash-shams', still written الـ.

cards.english: he is tired / she is tired (gender: ة)
cards.grammarNote:
Every noun and adjective is **masculine or feminine**; the feminine usually adds **ة** (taa marbuuta):
**هو تعبان / هي تعبانة** (he/she is tired), **طالب / طالبة** (male/female student). Adjectives agree with their noun.
cards.englishPhrase: He is a teacher, she is a teacher.

cards.grammarNote:
Possession is shown by **suffixes** attached to the noun:
**ـي** (my) **اسمي** (my name), **ـك** (your) **اسمك**, **ـه** (his) **اسمه**, **ـها** (her) **اسمها**. There's no separate word for 'my'.

Turn a statement into a yes/no question by adding **هل** (or **أ**) at the front:
**أنت طالب** → **هل أنت طالب؟** (are you a student?). Answer with **نعم** (yes) or **لا** (no).

produce.concept: هل turns a statement into a yes/no question
produce.answer: هل أنت طالب؟ hal anta talib?
produce.gloss: Put هل at the start; nothing else changes.

cards.grammarNote:
**أريد** (urid) = I want — followed directly by the thing:
**أريد ماءً** (I want water), **أريد قهوة** (I want a coffee). For 'I want to (do)', add a verb: **أريد أن آكل** (I want to eat).

cards.english: please (to a man / to a woman)
cards.grammarNote:
Politeness endings change with the listener's gender:
**من فضلك** (min fadlik, to a man) / **من فضلكِ** (min fadliki, to a woman). The same **ـك** vs **ـكِ** split shows up across 'your', commands, and greetings.

**أحب** (uhibb) = I like / love; for liking something in general, use the **definite** noun:
**أحب القهوة** (I like coffee), **أحب الشاي** (I like tea). Add a verb for 'like to do': **أحب أن أقرأ** (I like to read).

cards.english: The food is delicious. (adjective follows noun)
cards.grammarNote:
The **adjective comes after the noun** and agrees with it:
**الطعام لذيذ** (the food [is] delicious), **قهوة ساخنة** (hot coffee — fem. adds **ة**). A definite noun + indefinite adjective reads as a full sentence: 'the food is delicious'.

produce.concept: The adjective comes AFTER the noun (and agrees)
produce.gloss: Adjective follows the noun; agrees in gender & definiteness.

cards.english: I am at home. (في = in / at)
cards.grammarNote:
**في** (fi) = in / at — for being somewhere:
**أنا في البيت** (I'm at home), **هو في المدرسة** (he's at school). It's a nominal sentence: no 'am/is', just **في** + place.

produce.answer: أنا في البيت ana fi al-bayt

cards.english: on / under / next to (على / تحت / بجانب)
cards.grammarNote:
Common place prepositions, each followed by the noun:
**على** (on) **على الطاولة**, **تحت** (under) **تحت الكرسي**, **بجانب** (next to) **بجانب البنك**, **أمام** (in front of), **خلف** (behind).
cards.englishPhrase: The cat is under the table.

table.title: Common place prepositions
table.note: The noun after them usually takes الـ.

cards.grammarNote:
**هناك** (hunaka) = there is / there are (literally 'there'):
**هناك بنك قريب** (there's a bank nearby), **هناك مطاعم كثيرة** (there are many restaurants). Same form for singular and plural.

cards.english: I go to the park. (أذهب إلى …)
cards.grammarNote:
**إلى** (ila) = to / toward, used with motion verbs like **أذهب** (I go):
**أذهب إلى الحديقة** (I go to the park), **أذهب إلى العمل** (I go to work). The verb often comes first in the sentence.

cards.english: I am a doctor. (أنا طبيب — no 'am')
cards.grammarNote:
State a job as a nominal sentence, with gender agreement:
**أنا طبيب** (male) / **أنا طبيبة** (female), **هو مهندس** (he's an engineer). The feminine adds **ة**: **مهندسة**.

Present-tense verbs change with a **prefix**: **أ** (I), **ت** (you/she), **ي** (he), **ن** (we):
**أعمل** (I work), **تعمل** (you work), **يعمل** (he works), **نعمل** (we work). The stem **-عمل-** stays the same.

cards.english: I work in a hospital. (أعمل في / كـ)
cards.grammarNote:
**أعمل في** = I work in/at (a place); **أعمل كـ** = I work as (a role):
**أعمل في مستشفى** (I work in a hospital), **أعمل كطبيب** (I work as a doctor — **كـ** attaches to the word).

cloze.prompt: I work in a hospital. (in / at)

cards.grammarNote:
For hobbies, use **أحب** + the **verbal noun** (the 'act of…'), usually with **الـ**:
**أحب السباحة** (I like swimming), **أحب القراءة** (I like reading), **أحب الجري** (I like running).

produce.gloss: Use the noun form السباحة (swimming), with الـ.

cards.grammarNote:
Feelings are nominal sentences (no 'am'), and the adjective agrees in gender:
**أنا سعيد** (male) / **أنا سعيدة** (female) = I'm happy, **أنا حزين / حزينة** (I'm sad).

**أشعر بـ** (ash'ur bi-) = I feel + (a noun); **بـ** attaches to the following word:
**أشعر بالتعب** (I feel tired[ness]), **أشعر بالسعادة** (I feel happy[ness]), **أشعر بالخوف** (I feel fear).

cards.english: he is nervous / she is nervous (متوتر / متوترة)
cards.grammarNote:
Mood adjectives agree with the person's gender — feminine adds **ة**:
**متوتر / متوترة** (nervous), **غاضب / غاضبة** (angry), **متعب / متعبة** (tired). Match the adjective to who you're describing.

**جداً** (jiddan) = very — and it comes **after** the adjective, not before:
**متعب جداً** (very tired), **سعيد جداً** (very happy), **جميل جداً** (very beautiful).

Body parts take the same **possessive suffixes** as other nouns:
**يدي** (my hand), **يدك** (your hand), **رأسه** (his head), **عينها** (her eye). The **ـي** ending = 'my'.

table.title: Possessive suffix ـي = my
table.note: Attach ـي to the noun — there's no separate word for 'my'.

cards.grammarNote:
A common way to say something hurts: the body part (+ 'my') as subject + **يؤلمني** ('it pains me'):
**رأسي يؤلمني** (my head hurts), **بطني يؤلمني** (my stomach hurts). The verb agrees in gender: **يدي تؤلمني** (fem.).

produce.concept: Say what hurts: body part + يؤلمني (hurts me)

cards.grammarNote:
The adjective comes **after** the body part and agrees with it. Non-human plurals take a **feminine singular** adjective:
**عيون كبيرة** (big eyes), **يد قوية** (a strong hand), **شعر طويل** (long hair).

produce.concept: Adjective follows the noun and agrees
produce.gloss: Object plurals often take feminine-singular agreement.

cards.grammarNote:
Arabic has a special **dual** for exactly two — add **ـان** (or **ـين**): ideal for paired body parts:
**يد → يدان** (two hands), **عين → عينان** (two eyes), **رِجل → رِجلان** (two legs). No number word needed.

table.title: Singular · dual · plural
table.note: Arabic has a special dual form for exactly two.

packs.name: Equational Sentences — No Verb To Be

cards.grammarNote: Arabic drops the present-tense verb 'to be.' Simply place the subject next to the predicate. القهوة (the coffee) + ساخنة (hot, fem.) = 'The coffee is hot.' No linking verb needed.
أنا (I) + جائع (hungry, masc.) — the pronoun fills the 'subject' slot and the adjective fills the 'predicate' slot. Female speaker: أنا جائعة (ana ja'ia).

cards.english: My sister is a student at the university.
The weather was beautiful. (past tense — kana appears)
cards.grammarNote: Past tense 'to be' = كان (kana). Only present tense drops the verb. كان (kana) = was/were; كانت (kanat) = was (fem.); سيكون (sayakun) = will be (future).

cards.english: the happy man (noun phrase) vs. The man is happy. (sentence)
cards.grammarNote: Key distinction: الرجل السعيد (the happy man) = both definite, modifier. الرجل سعيد (The man is happy) = predicate adjective stays INDEFINITE. This definiteness difference is how you tell noun phrases from equational sentences.
Arabic drops 'to be' in the present. أنا (I) + سعيد (happy, masc.) = 'I am happy.' Female speaker: أنا سعيدة (ana sa'ida).
سعداء is the broken plural of سعيد. Arabic has two types of plural: sound (add ون/ات) and broken (internal vowel change).

cards.english: Count from zero to five in Arabic.
cards.word: صفر، واحد، اثنان، ثلاثة، أربعة، خمسة
cards.romanized: sifr, wāḥid, ithnān, thalātha, arbaʿa, khamsa.
cards.grammarNote: These are the cardinal numbers. 1 and 2 agree in gender with the noun they count. 3–10 use the opposite gender — that rule starts with ثلاثة/ثلاث.

cards.english: Count from six to ten in Arabic.
What is the gender reversal rule for Arabic numbers 3–10?
cards.word: Numbers 3–10 use the OPPOSITE gender of the noun they count.
cards.grammarNote: Masculine noun → feminine number (with ة). Feminine noun → masculine number (without ة). Example: ثلاثة كتب (three books, masc. noun → fem. number) vs. ثلاث بنات (three girls, fem. noun → masc. number).
كتاب (kitāb = book) is masculine, so the number takes the feminine form ثلاثة (with ة). The counted noun appears in the plural: كتب (kutub).
بنت (bint = girl) is feminine, so the number takes the masculine form ثلاث (without ة). The counted noun is plural: بنات (banāt).
أصدقاء (aṣdiqāʾ = friends) is masculine plural, so the number is feminine: خمسة (khamsa, with ة).
Compound numbers above 20 put the unit first: واحد وعشرون = 'one and twenty' = 21. The و (wa = and) connects them.
مئة (miʾa) = 100. ألف (alf) = 1000. To say 200: مئتان (miʾatān, dual form). To say 2000: ألفان (alfān).
Time uses ordinal numbers: الثانية (the second), الثالثة (the third), etc. الساعة (al-sāʿa) = the clock/hour. No verb needed — this is an equational sentence.
النصف (al-niṣf) = the half. الربع (al-rubʿ) = the quarter. So: الثالثة والربع = 3:15 (three and a quarter).
تذاكر (tadhākir = tickets) is feminine, so the number is masculine: ثلاث (thalāth, without ة).
اليوم (al-yawm) = today. Can open or close the sentence: اليوم أنا مشغول (Today I am busy) or أنا مشغول اليوم (I am busy today). Both are natural.
الآن (al-ān) = now (formal and colloquial). بعدين (baʿdain) = later, very common in colloquial Arabic. The formal equivalent is لاحقاً (lāḥiqan).
قبل (qabl) and بعد (baʿd) can stand alone as adverbs or precede a noun: قبل الغداء (qabl al-ghadāʾ = before lunch), بعد العمل (baʿd al-ʿamal = after work).

cards.english: What day does the Arabic week start on?
cards.grammarNote: The Arabic week runs Sunday (الأحد) through Saturday (السبت). Friday (الجمعة) is the day of communal prayer and is the primary day off in many Arab countries.
الجمعة comes from جمع (jam = gathering/congregation). Friday is the most culturally significant weekday — صلاة الجمعة (ṣalāt al-jumʿa) is the obligatory Friday noon prayer.
To say 'on [day],' use يوم (yawm = day of) before the day name, or simply use the day name with the definite article: الاثنين = on Monday.
أبداً (abadan = never) must be paired with a negated verb: لا أذهب أبداً (lā adhhab abadan = I never go). Alone in response to a question, أبداً means 'absolutely not.'

cards.english: I always drink coffee in the morning.
كِتَاب means ___ and comes from root ___
cards.grammarNote: كِتَاب (kitāb) follows the CiCāC pattern — a common shape for abstract or object nouns. The three consonants ك، ت، ب are the skeleton; the vowels i and ā give it its noun shape.

cards.english: What does the pattern CāCiC (فَاعِل) mean?
cards.word: Active participle — the doer of the action. e.g., كَاتِب (kātib) = writer, عَامِل (ʿāmil) = worker, دَارِس (dāris) = student/studier
cards.grammarNote: The CāCiC pattern is one of the most productive in Arabic. Spot it by the long ā vowel after the first root consonant and a kasra (i) under the second. It always means 'the one who does X.'

cards.word: Root د-ر-س (d-r-s) = studying/learning. مَدْرَسَة (madrasa) = school — a place of studying.
cards.grammarNote: مَدْرَسَة follows the maCCaCa pattern — a place-noun template. The م prefix + root + short a vowels = 'the place where this root's action happens.' Same pattern as مَكْتَبَة (maktaba, library/bookstore).

cards.word: مَكْتُوب (maktūb) = written / a letter — something that has been written.
cards.grammarNote: The maCCūC (مَفْعُول) pattern is the passive participle across virtually all roots. The long ū vowel on the third consonant is the key marker. Compare: مَكْتَب (maktab, office — place noun, short a) vs. مَكْتُوب (maktūb, written — passive, long ū).

cards.english: What root do كَتَبَ، كِتَاب، كَاتِب، and مَكْتَبَة all share?
cards.word: Root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b) = writing. All four words contain the consonants ك، ت، ب in that order.
cards.grammarNote: To find the root, strip away the vowels and any م prefix. What consonants remain, in order? That is your root. كِتَاب → ك ت ب. مَكْتَبَة → (drop م) → ك ت ب.

cards.english: What role does the maCCaC / maCCaCa pattern play?
cards.word: Place of action noun. مَكْتَب (maktab) = office/desk, مَدْرَسَة (madrasa) = school, مَعْمَل (maʿmal) = laboratory.
cards.grammarNote: Any word starting with م followed by a root's consonants with short a vowels is likely a place noun. The feminine ending ـة often appears on place nouns too: مَكْتَبَة (library), مَدْرَسَة (school).

cards.word: دَرَسَ (darasa) = he studied. Pattern: CaCaCa (فَعَلَ) — the standard Form I past tense verb pattern.
cards.grammarNote: The CaCaCa pattern (three short a vowels across three root consonants) is the most common Form I past tense shape. كَتَبَ (kataba, he wrote), دَرَسَ (darasa, he studied), عَمِلَ (ʿamila, he worked — slight variant with i on the second vowel).

cards.english: عَامِل (ʿāmil) means ___ and shares its pattern with ___
cards.word: عَامِل (ʿāmil) = worker/factor. CāCiC pattern — same as كَاتِب (kātib, writer) and دَارِس (dāris, studier).
cards.grammarNote: Root ع-م-ل (ʿ-m-l) = work/doing. عَامِل is the active participle: long ā after ع, kasra under م. The CāCiC pattern reliably produces the 'doer' meaning across all roots.

cards.english: مُدَرِّس (mudarris) means ___ — why does it look different from دَارِس?
cards.word: مُدَرِّس (mudarris) = teacher. The doubled middle consonant (رّ) signals Form II — an intensive/causative form. A mudarris is one who causes others to study.
cards.grammarNote: Form II verbs double the middle root consonant and use the prefix مُـ in their active participle. مُدَرِّس (teacher) vs. دَارِس (studier/student). Form II often means 'to cause X' or 'to do X intensively,' so the doer is frequently a teacher, trainer, or professional.

cards.english: كُتُب (kutub) is the plural of كِتَاب. What type of plural is this?
cards.word: Broken plural (جمع التكسير, jamʿ al-taksīr) — the vowel pattern changes rather than adding a suffix. كِتَاب → كُتُب.
cards.grammarNote: Arabic often forms plurals by changing internal vowels rather than adding endings — these are called broken plurals. There are many patterns; CuCuC (كُتُب, كُتُب) is one common one. Broken plurals must often be memorised per word, but seeing the same root consonants tells you what the plural means.

cards.english: مَعْمَل (maʿmal) comes from root ___ and means ___
cards.word: Root ع-م-ل (ʿ-m-l) = work/doing. مَعْمَل (maʿmal) = laboratory / factory — the place where work is done.
cards.grammarNote: maCCaC place-noun pattern at work again: م + ع-م-ل + short a vowels = a place of work. Same template as مَكْتَب (office, from writing root) and the implied place-nouns from dozens of other roots.

cards.english: You see an unfamiliar Arabic word. What is the first thing to look for?
cards.word: The 3-consonant root skeleton. Strip vowels and affixes (especially a leading م). Identify the three consonants in order — they point to the core meaning.
cards.grammarNote: Arabic has hundreds of roots. Once you know a root, you can often guess 8–10 related words. The patterns — CaCaCa (past verb), CāCiC (doer), maCCaC (place), maCCūC (passive), CiCāC (noun) — repeat across every root. Learn the patterns once; apply them everywhere.
أنا (ana) = I, used for both masculine and feminine speakers. In Arabic, the verb conjugation already encodes the subject, so أنا is often omitted in speech but used for emphasis.
Arabic distinguishes gender in 'you': أنتَ (anta) for masculine, أنتِ (anti) for feminine. The difference is a fatha (ـَ) vs kasra (ـِ) on the ت.
أنتِ (anti) = you (feminine). The kasra under the ت distinguishes it from أنتَ (anta = you, masculine). In unvowelled text they look identical — context and gender of the listener clarify.
هو (huwa) = he, and also 'it' for masculine nouns. Arabic has no neuter pronoun — every noun is masculine or feminine. الكتاب (the book) is masculine, so 'it' = هو.
هي (hiya) = she, and also 'it' for feminine nouns. الطاولة (the table) is feminine, so 'it' = هي.
نحن (nahnu) = we, used for both mixed and same-gender groups. The verb form for 'we' always begins with نـ (n-): نكتب (naktub = we write).
هم (hum) = they, for all-male or mixed-gender groups. The default plural pronoun. هن (hunna) is used for all-female groups.
Arabic has a special dual form for exactly two people or things. هما (huma) = the two of them. This is unique among major world languages. Dual also exists for nouns: كتابان (kitaban) = two books.
Equational sentence: no verb 'to be' in present tense. أنا (I) + طالب (student, masc.) = 'I am a student.' If the speaker is female: أنا طالبة (ana taaliba).
Arabic distinguishes masculine and feminine in 2nd person. anta (to a man), anti (to a woman).
The possessive suffix also changes: -ak (masc.) vs -ik (fem.). كيف حالك (to man) / كيف حالِك (to woman).
بخير (bikhyr) = well/fine. الحمد لله (al-hamdu lillah) = praise be to God — the standard positive response in Arabic.
ذَهَبَ (dhahaba) is the base form of the past tense — 3rd person masculine singular. The pattern فَعَلَ (fa'ala) with vowels a-a-a is the most common Form I past tense pattern.
Adding ـتْ (-at) to the base form creates the 3rd person feminine singular past. The taa' marbuta ت is written with sukuun (ـتْ) at the end of a sentence.
The 1st person singular past is formed by adding ـتُ (-tu) to the verb stem. The stem vowel drops: ذَهَبَ → ذَهَبْتُ.
The 1st person plural past is formed by adding ـنَا (-na) to the verb stem.
قَالَ (qala) is an irregular verb — it has a long vowel ā in the stem. The root is ق-و-ل. In 1st person: قُلْتُ (qultu), the long vowel shortens and the vowel changes.
قُلْتُ (qultu) shows the stem change in hollow verbs: the long ā shortens and the vowel changes to u when a consonant suffix is added.
فَعَلَ (fa'ala) = he did/made. This word is also the Arabic grammatical template verb — the root ف-ع-ل represents any generic verb root in grammar explanations.
جداً (jiddan) = very. It always follows the adjective: كبير جداً (very big), not جداً كبير. The ً is a tanwin sound (-an), always written with جداً.

cards.english: I am very happy to meet you.

cards.grammarNote: شكراً جزيلاً = thank you very much (literally: abundant thanks). جزيلاً is an alternative to جداً for intensifying certain expressions.

cards.english: This is too spicy for me.

cards.grammarNote: أعجبني (a'jabani) = it pleased me / I liked it. كثيراً = very much. A common way to express strong approval.
أبداً (abadan) = at all / never. Used in negative sentences for emphasis.

cards.english: I like this job very much.

cards.grammarNote: جداً does not change for gender — it always stays جداً regardless of masculine or feminine context.
شوية (shwayya) = a little, a bit — very common in spoken Arabic. تعبان شوية = a little tired.
أبداً (abadan) = not at all / never, used in negative sentences: ما أريده أبداً (I don't want it at all).
كتير (ktir) = very or a lot in Levantine Arabic. كتير منيح = very good. أكل كتير = ate a lot.
Doubling جداً jiddan jiddan is common in spoken Arabic to mean 'extremely'. More formal: بالغاية (bil-ghaya).
Possession in Arabic is expressed by attaching a suffix directly to the noun. ـِي (-ī) = my. The noun loses its tanwin (nunation) when a suffix is added: بَيْت + ي = بَيْتِي.
ـكَ (-ka) = your (masculine). The case ending of the noun (here -u nominative) shows before the suffix: اِسْمُ + كَ = اِسْمُكَ.
ـكِ (-ki) = your (feminine). The only difference from the masculine suffix ـكَ is the kasra vowel, giving ـكِ. In unvowelled text they look identical — context clarifies.
ـهُ (-hu) = his. After a nominative noun the suffix is -hu: صَدِيقُهُ. After a genitive noun: صَدِيقِهِ (-hi). The vowel on the suffix harmonizes with the preceding vowel.
ـهَا (-hā) = her. Unlike the masculine suffix, the feminine 3rd person suffix does not change with case: always -hā.
ـنَا (-nā) = our. This suffix is the same for all genders and is invariable: بَيْتُنَا (our house), كِتَابُنَا (our book).
ـكُمْ (-kum) = your (masculine plural). For a feminine plural group: ـكُنَّ (-kunna). ـكُمْ is the default form used in MSA for mixed or unspecified groups.
ـهُمْ (-hum) = their (masculine/mixed group). For a feminine-only group: ـهُنَّ (-hunna). Compare: بَيْتُهُمْ (their house, mixed group) vs بَيْتُهُنَّ (their house, women only).
أَب (father) is one of five special nouns whose vowel changes with case: أَبُوكَ (nominative), أَبَاكَ (accusative), أَبِيكَ (genitive). These are called the Five Nouns (الأسماء الخمسة).
When adding a suffix to a feminine noun ending in ة (taa' marbuta), the ة becomes ت: لُغَة + نَا = لُغَتُنَا. The taa' marbuta always 'opens up' before a suffix.
لا (la) negates nouns and adjectives in equational sentences, and is used for the present tense with verbs in MSA. Also simply means 'no' in response.
ما (ma) is common in Egyptian/Levantine Arabic to negate present verbs: ما أعرفش = I don't know. In MSA لا is used for verb negation.
لن (lan) negates future actions: لن أذهب = I will not go. Requires the subjunctive verb form in MSA.
لا + present tense verb = 'does not / do not.' Very common in conversation.
لست (lastu) = I am not. لست is the negation of كنت — used to negate 'to be' sentences in past or present formal Arabic.
Prohibition (don't): لا + jussive verb form. لا تذهب (to a man), لا تذهبي (to a woman).
ليس (laysa) = is not. Used to negate nouns and adjectives: ليس + predicate.
لا (la) as a standalone word = no. The opposite of نعم (na'am = yes). لا alone is direct; adding شكراً softens the refusal.
ما (ma) is used in Levantine Arabic to negate past-tense verbs. Very common in everyday speech: ما أكلت (I didn't eat), ما عرفت (I didn't know), ما جيت (I didn't come). In MSA, past negation uses لم.
ما في (ma fi) = there is no... in Levantine Arabic. Extremely common. ما في حدا (no one is here), ما في وقت (there's no time). This is equivalent to MSA لا يوجد (la yujad).

لم (lam) + present-tense verb form = past negation in MSA. The verb after لم uses the present form but means past: لم أذهب (I did not go), لم يأكل (he did not eat). لم is formal — you'll see it in news, writing, and formal speech.
لن (lan) + present verb = will not (future negation). لن أذهب (I will not go), لن يأتي (he will not come). Used in both MSA and educated speech.

cards.english: He is not a doctor. (formal — laysa)
cards.grammarNote: ليس (laysa) = is not, negates equational sentences formally. ليس طبيباً (he is not a doctor — note the accusative ending on طبيباً). Feminine: ليست (laysat). Colloquial alternative: مش (mish) in Levantine.

مش (mish) = not, negates adjectives and nouns in Levantine colloquial Arabic. مش كويس (mish kuwayyis = not good), مش هون (mish hun = not here), مش صحيح (mish sahih = not correct). Very frequent in everyday Levantine speech.

أبداً (abadan) = never, used after لا + verb: لا أتأخر أبداً (I never arrive late). As a standalone answer: أبداً! = Absolutely not!/Never! Also: لم + verb + قط (qatt) = never did in the past: لم أذهب قط (I have never gone).
لا negates verbs in the present tense: لا أشعر بألم (I don't feel pain). Also used as a standalone 'no.'
ليس (laysa) negates equational sentences. ليس + noun/adj = is not. لست (lastu) = I am not.
لا + indefinite noun = there is no X. لا ألم = no pain / there is no pain.
ليست is the feminine form of ليس. Used when the subject is feminine.
لا يوجد / لا توجد = there is no (masc./fem.). لديّ = at me / I have (prepositional possessive).
ال (al-) = 'the.' It attaches directly to the noun with no space. كتاب (kitab) = a book; الكتاب (al-kitab) = the book. Arabic has no word for 'a/an' — an indefinite noun has no article.
Sun letter: ط (ta') causes the 'l' in ال to assimilate. الطعام is written al-ta'am but pronounced at-ta'am. The spelling never changes — only the pronunciation.
Sun letter: د (dal) assimilates the 'l' of ال. Written al-dajaj, pronounced ad-dajaj.
Classic example of a sun letter: ش (shin) assimilates the 'l.' Written ال + شمس but pronounced ash-shams, not al-shams. The sun letters include: ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن.
No article = indefinite: قهوة (qahwa) = a coffee. Compare: القهوة (al-qahwa) = the coffee. The difference between 'a coffee' and 'the coffee' is simply the presence or absence of ال.
Arabic uses ال for generic categories: أحب الخبز (I like bread/the bread = bread in general). Unlike English which uses no article for generics, Arabic often uses ال.
When an adjective modifies a definite noun, the adjective also takes ال: الخبز (def.) + الطازج (def.) = 'the fresh bread.' Compare: خبز طازج (indefinite) = 'fresh bread.'
Moon letters (حروف قمرية) do NOT assimilate the 'l' of ال. م (mim) is a moon letter, so المستشفى is pronounced al-mustashfa (with clear 'l'). Moon letters: أ ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي.
الـ (al-) attaches to the word. Before 'sun letters' (ت د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن), the ل of al- assimilates: الشارع → ash-shāri'. Before 'moon letters' (all others), it stays: البيت → al-bayt.
السوق: س is a sun letter, so al- assimilates to as-. Pronounced as-sūq.
الشارع: ش is a sun letter — al- becomes ash-. Pronounced ash-shāri'.
أين (ayn) = where. Arabic drops 'to be' in the present: just 'where (is) the hospital?'
يـ prefix marks masculine singular present. أكَلَ (akala) is the root (he ate). Present tense: يأكل (he eats), تأكل (she eats / you eat), أكل (I eat).
First person present: أ (a-) prefix. أكل = I eat. أشرب = I drink.

cards.english: I drink coffee in the morning.

cards.grammarNote: تـ prefix marks feminine/you present: تطبخ = she cooks / you cook.

cards.english: What do you eat for breakfast?

cards.grammarNote: نـ prefix marks plural first person (we): نأكل = we eat.
يشربون = they drink (masc. plural). The ون suffix marks masculine plural in the present.
Present tense prefix for 'I' (أنا) = أـ (a-). So كتب (the root k-t-b) → أكتب (aktub = I write). This prefix applies to all verbs: أذهب (I go), أعمل (I work), أدرس (I study).
Present tense prefix for 'he' (هو) = يـ (y-). يكتب (yaktub = he writes). This same prefix is used for 'they (m.)': يكتبون (yaktubun = they write).
Present tense prefix for 'she' (هي) = تـ (t-). Also used for 'you (m.)': تكتب (taktub). Context and the stated pronoun distinguish between 'she writes' and 'you (m.) write.'
Present tense prefix for 'we' (نحن) = نـ (n-). نكتب (naktub = we write). Easy to remember: نحن starts with ن, and so does the verb prefix.
Note تتكلم for 'she speaks' — both the prefix تـ AND the verb starts with تـ, so you get two تـ: ت (prefix) + تكلم (verb) = تتكلم.

cards.english: We go to the office every day.

cards.grammarNote: Arabic present tense covers both 'I learn' and 'I am learning.' There is no separate progressive form. أتعلّم means both.

cards.english: From root ك-ت-ب: book, office, writer, library
cards.grammarNote: Arabic verbs share roots (جذور, judur) with related nouns. The root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b) relates to writing: كتب (he wrote), يكتب (he writes), كتاب (book), مكتب (office/desk), كاتب (writer), مكتبة (library). Learning roots multiplies vocabulary.
كَثِير (kathīr) = a lot/much. When followed by a specific noun, use مِن (min, 'of'): كَثِير مِن الْمَاء. كَثِيرًا is the adverbial form: شَكَرًا كَثِيرًا (thank you very much).
قَلِيل (qalīl) = a little/few. Opposite of كَثِير. Also used adverbially: تَكَلَّمْ قَلِيلًا (speak a little). For uncountable nouns use مِن + the noun with the definite article.
بَعْض (baʿḍ) = some/part of. It is followed directly by a definite noun (with الـ) in the genitive: بَعْض الطَّعَام (some food). Unlike كَثِير and قَلِيل, it does not use مِن.

كِلَا (kilā) = both (for dual masculine), كِلْتَا (kiltā) = both (for dual feminine). Always followed by a dual noun in the genitive. كِلَا الطَّبَقَيْنِ = both dishes (lit. 'both of the two dishes').
نِصْف (niṣf) = half. Directly precedes the noun without مِن: نِصْف كِيلُو (half a kilo), نِصْف سَاعَة (half an hour). The following noun is in the genitive case.
كَافٍ (kāfin) = sufficient/enough, an adjective that follows the noun and agrees in gender. Alternatively: يَكْفِي الطَّعَام (the food is sufficient) using the verb كَفَى.
When نِصْف is followed by a definite noun, the noun takes the definite article الـ: نِصْف الْوَجْبَة (half the meal). When indefinite: نِصْف وَجْبَة (half a meal).
Arabic nouns are either masculine (مذكر, mudhakkar) or feminine (مؤنث, mu'annath). Most masculine nouns have no special ending. Add ة to get the feminine form: طالب → طالبة.
The ة (ta marbuta) ending is the clearest marker of a feminine noun. It is pronounced as '-a' in isolation and '-at' when followed by another word in a genitive construction.
Adjectives also have masculine and feminine forms. The adjective must agree with the noun it describes: بيت كبير (a big house, masc.), غرفة كبيرة (a big room, fem.).

cards.english: bread (masculine noun — adjective must be masc.)
cards.grammarNote: خبز (bread) is masculine, so its adjectives use the masculine form: خبز طازج (fresh bread). قهوة (coffee) is feminine: قهوة طازجة (fresh coffee).

cards.english: coffee (feminine noun — adjective must be fem.)

cards.grammarNote: When describing yourself, the adjective must match your gender: أنا سعيد (male), أنا سعيدة (female). The same applies to all predicative adjectives in equational sentences.
Some nouns are feminine without the ة ending — usually because of natural gender or convention. أم (umm = mother), بنت (bint = girl), شمس (shams = sun), أرض (ard = earth). These must be memorized.
وجبة (meal) ends in ة, so it's feminine. Its adjective لذيذ becomes لذيذة. Always check the noun's gender before choosing the adjective form.

cards.english: Feminine nouns usually end in ة (ta marbuta).
cards.grammarNote: Most feminine nouns end in ة (pronounced -a). Professions often follow this: طبيب (male doctor) / طبيبة (female doctor). Some nouns are feminine without ة (يد hand, أم mother, أرض earth).
كَانَ (kāna) is the past tense of 'to be'. It is a كَانَ-sister (فعل ناقص): it takes a nominative subject and an accusative predicate. The adjective لَذِيذًا is in the accusative (tanwin -an).
كَانَتْ (kānat) is the feminine form of كَانَ. The predicate adjective سَاخِنَةً agrees with the subject in gender (feminine) and is in the accusative case.

cards.english: She used to cook every day.
cards.grammarNote: كَانَ + present tense verb expresses habitual past ('used to'). كَانَتْ تَطْبُخُ = she used to cook / she would cook. The present tense verb following كَانَ does not change its form.
كُنْتُ (kuntu) = I was / I used to. The 1st person singular of كَانَ. Full conjugation: كَانَ (he was), كَانَتْ (she was), كُنْتُ (I was), كُنَّا (we were), كُنْتَ (you were, m.).

كَانُوا (kānū) = they were (masculine plural). The plural predicate adjective جَائِعِينَ is in the accusative plural. Note: for inanimate plural nouns, the singular feminine form is used: كَانَتِ الأَطْبَاقُ نَظِيفَةً (the plates were clean).

cards.english: The market used to be busy.

cards.grammarNote: هَلْ (hal) turns a statement into a yes/no question. It comes before the verb. هَلْ كَانَ...؟ = was there...? كَانَ هُنَاكَ (kāna hunāka) = there was (lit. 'was there').
أَيْنَ (ayna) = where. In equational questions (no verb), the question word is followed directly by the subject: أَيْنَ الْحَمَّامُ؟ (lit. 'where the bathroom?'). No verb needed.

cards.english: How do I get to the station?
cards.grammarNote: كَيْفَ (kayfa) = how. Followed by a verb: كَيْفَ + verb phrase. أَصِلُ (aṣilu) = I reach/get to, from the verb وَصَلَ (waṣala). Note إِلَى (ilā) = to, for destinations.
مَتَى (matā) = when. Used for questions about time. Not to be confused with مَا (mā) = what.
لِمَاذَا (limādhā) = why (lit. 'for what'). لِ (li) = for/because of + مَاذَا (mādhā) = what. In speech, لِيه (lēh) is the colloquial equivalent heard in Egyptian Arabic.
مَنْ (man) = who. Used for people. Do not confuse with مِن (min) = from (different vowel). مَنْ هَذَا؟ = who is this? مَنْ أَنْت؟ = who are you?
مَا (mā) = what (for definitions/identities). مَاذَا (mādhā) = what (for actions with verbs): مَاذَا تَفْعَل؟ (what are you doing?). مَا هَذَا؟ = what is this?
كَمْ (kam) = how much / how many / how far. Used for quantity and distance. كَمْ يَكْلُف؟ = how much does it cost? كَمْ الْمَسَافَة؟ = how far is the distance?

cards.english: Which bus goes to the center?
cards.grammarNote: أَيّ (ayy) = which/what kind of. It is followed by a noun in the nominative. أَيُّ (with nominative ending -u) before the noun: أَيُّ حَافِلَة = which bus.

الإضافة (iḍāfa) is the Arabic construct for possession/relationship between two nouns. Rules: (1) the first noun has no article, (2) the second noun is in the genitive case (kasra ending), (3) the first noun's definiteness is determined by the second.
When the second noun has الـ, the entire iḍāfa construct is definite: وَسَطُ الْمَدِينَةِ = the center of the city (definite). Without الـ: وَسَطُ مَدِينَةٍ = a center of a city (indefinite).
A three-word iḍāfa chain is possible: مَدْخَلُ مَطَارِ الْمَدِينَةِ (entrance of the city's airport). Only the very last noun can have الـ or a possessive suffix.
A three-noun iḍāfa chain: تَذْكِرَةُ (ticket of) + دُخُولِ (entrance of) + الْمُتْحَف (the museum). Each intermediate noun is in the genitive, and only the last noun carries الـ.
في (fi) = in, at, inside. Used for being inside a place: في البيت (in the house). Also used for time: في الصباح (in the morning). One of the most frequently used Arabic words.
على ('ala) = on, on top of. الكتاب على الطاولة (the book is on the table). Contrast with في (inside): في الحقيبة (in the bag) vs على الحقيبة (on the bag).
من (min) = from, of. أنا من الأردن (I am from Jordan). Also used in phrases: من فضلك (please, lit. 'from your grace').
إلى (ila) = to, toward. نذهب إلى المطعم (we go to the restaurant). Used for direction and destination.
عن ('an) = about, concerning; also 'away from.' يبحث عن (yabhath 'an = to search for/about). تحدّث عن (tahaddath 'an = to talk about).
بـ (bi-) attaches directly to the next word with no space. بالسيارة (by car), بالعربية (in Arabic), بسرعة (quickly, lit. 'with speed'). Very common preposition.
لـ (li-) attaches to the next word: هذا لك (this is for you), لي (for me/mine). Also appears in lil- (for the): لِلمطعم (for/to the restaurant).

cards.english: The keys are in the bag.
The cat is under the table.
The bank is next to the cafe.

cards.grammarNote: Pattern: Subject + في + Place (no verb 'to be' in present tense). أنا في البيت = 'I [am] in the house.' The equational sentence structure makes this very direct.

cards.english: The book is in the bag.

cards.grammarNote: في is used for time expressions too: في الصباح (in the morning), في المساء (in the evening), في الليل (at night), في الصيف (in summer). Very versatile preposition.
أين (ayna) = where? The answer uses في: الحمام في النهاية (the bathroom is at the end). Questions with أين always expect a location answer, often featuring في.

cards.english: Where do you live? — I live in Damascus.
The sandwich has cheese in it.
cards.grammarNote: فيها (fiha) = 'in it' (feminine). في + ها (her/it-fem.) = فيها. Masculine: فيه (fihi). These contracted forms are very common: الحساء فيه ملح كثير (the soup has a lot of salt in it).

cards.english: The soup has a lot of salt in it.

cards.grammarNote: في أمان الله (fi aman allah) = a traditional Islamic parting, lit. 'in God's protection.' Shows how في is used idiomatically beyond just physical location.

الَّذِي (alladhī) = who/which/that (masculine singular). It follows a definite antecedent (الطَّبِيبُ) and agrees with it in gender and number. The verb in the relative clause agrees with the antecedent.

When the relative pronoun is the object of a preposition, a resumptive pronoun is required: بِهِ (bihi = by it/with it). الَّذِي أَقُومُ بِهِ = that I carry out (lit. 'that I stand with it'). This pronoun refers back to الْعَمَل.
Past tense is common in relative clauses. سَاعَدَنِي = helped me (سَاعَدَ + نِي suffix). The relative clause modifies الزَّمِيل (the colleague, masculine), so الَّذِي is used.

cards.english: the nurse who cares for patients (feminine)
cards.grammarNote: الَّتِي (allatī) = who/which/that (feminine singular). Agrees with الْمُمَرِّضَةُ (nurse, feminine). The four main relative pronouns: الَّذِي (m.s.), الَّتِي (f.s.), الَّذِينَ (m.pl.), اللَّوَاتِي / اللَّائِي (f.pl.).

cards.english: the engineers who designed the building
cards.grammarNote: الَّذِينَ (alladhīna) = who/which/that (masculine plural). Used for people. For inanimate plural nouns, use the singular feminine form الَّتِي: الْكُتُبُ الَّتِي قَرَأْتُهَا (the books that I read).

When the relative pronoun is the direct object of the relative clause verb, a resumptive pronoun is added to the verb: أُحِبُّهَا (I love it, f.). The هَا refers back to الْوَظِيفَةُ (the job, feminine).

cards.english: the student who passed the exam

cards.grammarNote: فِيهَا (fīhā) = in it (feminine). The preposition فِي (in) + هَا (it/her) forms the resumptive pronoun phrase, required when the relative pronoun is the object of a preposition in the relative clause.

cards.english: the office that I work in
the women who applied for the job
cards.grammarNote: اللَّوَاتِي (allawātī) = who/which (feminine plural, for people). Also اللَّائِي (allāʾī). For female humans specifically. تَقَدَّمْنَ = they applied (3rd person feminine plural past).

packs.name: المستقبل — Future Tense with سـ / سوف

cards.grammarNote: The future is formed by prefixing سَـ (sa-) directly to the present tense verb: سَـ + أَعْمَلُ = سَأَعْمَلُ. سَـ is short and informal; سَوْفَ (sawfa) is the formal/emphatic alternative: سَوْفَ أَعْمَل.
سَـ + تَدْرُسُ (she studies) = سَتَدْرُسُ (she will study). The present tense verb form is identical to the future — only the سَـ prefix changes the meaning to future.
To form a yes/no question, add هَلْ (hal) before the verb: هَلْ سَتَأْتِي؟ The verb سَتَأْتِي = you will come (2nd person m. singular). هَلْ never changes.
لَنْ (lan) = will not (emphatic future negation). It is followed by the subjunctive: أَذْهَبَ (not أَذْهَبُ). Do not use سَـ with لَنْ — they cannot combine. لَنْ أَذْهَبَ = I will absolutely not go.
سَـ + يُسَافِرُ (he travels) = سَيُسَافِرُ (he will travel). الأُسْبُوعَ الْقَادِم = next week (the coming week), in the accusative as a time adverb.

cards.english: The company will open a new branch.
cards.grammarNote: سَوْفَ (sawfa) is the formal/written version of سَـ, used in news, official announcements, and formal speech. It is written as a separate word before the present-tense verb. Both mean 'will'.
لَنْ + subjunctive + أَبَدًا (abadan, never/ever) is used for strong emphatic future negation. لَنْ تَسْتَسْلِمَ = she will not surrender (subjunctive form of تَسْتَسْلِمُ).

cards.english: rule: adjectives follow the noun and match its gender
cards.grammarNote: In Arabic, adjectives come AFTER the noun and must agree in gender (masc./fem.) and definiteness. Masculine base + ة makes it feminine.
Add ة (ta marbuta) to the masculine adjective to make it feminine: كبير → كبيرة. This rule applies to most regular adjectives.
كتاب (book) is masculine, so the adjective كبير stays masculine. Both noun and adjective are indefinite (no ال).
طاولة (table) is feminine (ends in ة), so the adjective becomes كبيرة. Noun feminine → adjective feminine.
When the noun is definite (has ال), the adjective also gets ال. Both take the definite article: الكتاب الكبير (the big book).
سيارة (car) is feminine → جديدة (new, fem.). Adjective agrees with the noun's gender.
ماء (water) is masculine, so the adjective بارد (cold) stays masculine.
When an adjective is the predicate (X is Y), the noun takes ال but the adjective does NOT: الكتاب جديد (the book is new). Compare: الكتاب الجديد = 'the new book' (modifying).

cards.english: Adjectives agree in gender and definiteness.
cards.grammarNote: Arabic adjectives match the noun in gender (masc/fem), number (sing/plural), and definiteness (definite/indefinite). Most fem. adjectives add ة (a).
يد (hand) is feminine, so the adjective is كبيرة (kabira), not كبير (kabir).
رأس (head) is masculine, so the adjective is كبير (kabir).
When definite, both noun and adjective take الـ: اليد الكبيرة (the big hand).
ألم (pain) is masculine, so شديد (severe/intense) matches: شديد not شديدة.
رجل (leg) is feminine in Arabic, so the adjective متورمة (swollen) takes the fem. ending ة.
صحة (health) is feminine — جيدة (good, fem.) matches.
Predicate adjectives agree with the subject. Male speaker: متعب (muta'ab). Female speaker: أنا متعبة (muta'aba).

packs.name: كَانَ + صِفَة — Past States with كَانَ

cards.grammarNote: كَانَ + adjective describes a past state. The adjective is in the accusative case (tanwin -an): سَعِيدًا, not سَعِيدٌ. This is because كَانَ is a verb that governs an accusative predicate (خَبَر كَانَ).
The predicate adjective agrees with the subject in gender: كَانَتْ (she was, f.) + حَزِينَةً (sad, f. accusative). The feminine accusative indefinite ends in ـَةً (-atan).
كَانُوا (kānū) = they were (masculine/mixed plural). The plural accusative adjective مُتْعَبِينَ ends in ـِينَ (-īna), the sound masculine plural accusative/genitive ending.
كُنْتُ (kuntu) = I was. The 1st person singular of كَانَ. The adjective خَائِفًا (afraid, m.) is in the accusative. A female speaker would say: كُنْتُ خَائِفَةً (kuntu khāʾifatan).
كُنَّا (kunnā) = we were. The plural predicate adjective مُتَحَمِّسِينَ takes the masculine plural accusative form. If a group of women: كُنَّا مُتَحَمِّسَاتٍ (sound feminine plural).
Negation of كَانَ + adjective: كَانَ غَيْرَ + adjective (lit. 'was other-than'). Or: لَمْ يَكُنْ مُرْتَاحًا (lam yakun murtāḥan) = he was not comfortable, using لَمْ + jussive of كَانَ.

سُعَدَاءَ (suʿadāʾa) is the broken plural of سَعِيد. Many Arabic adjectives form their plurals through internal vowel changes (broken plural) rather than adding a suffix. سُعَدَاءَ is accusative (no tanwin for words ending in ء preceded by alif).

cards.english: If I were happy, I would sing.
cards.grammarNote: لَوْ (law) introduces counterfactual (unreal) conditions. Pattern: لَوْ + past tense → لَـ + past tense. The لَـ in the result clause is a marker of the counterfactual. This describes something contrary to current reality.

cards.english: If you are sad, talk to me.
cards.grammarNote: إِذَا (idhā) introduces real conditions — things that could actually happen. Pattern: إِذَا + past/present → result. The result clause can be a command (imperative): تَكَلَّمْ (talk!). إِذَا ≠ لَوْ: إِذَا is real, لَوْ is unreal.

إِذَا كُنْتَ (idhā kunta) = if you are (lit. 'if you were'). Arabic uses the past tense in conditional clauses even for present/future real conditions. اِسْتَرِحْ is the imperative of اِسْتَرَاحَ (to rest).

cards.english: If I were rich, I would travel.
cards.grammarNote: لَوْ + كَانَ (past of 'to be') is the classic counterfactual structure. غَنِيًّا is accusative predicate of كَانَ. لَسَافَرْتُ = I would have traveled. The لَـ prefix on the result clause signals the unreal condition.

cards.english: If you feel better, we will go out.
If I had known, I wouldn't have come.
cards.grammarNote: لَوْ عَلِمْتُ = if I had known. لَمَا (la-mā) = (then) not: لَـ (result marker) + مَا (not, for past negation). This is a past counterfactual — neither condition nor result happened.

cards.english: If you feel nervous, breathe deeply.
If she were here, she would be happy.
cards.grammarNote: لَوْ كَانَتْ ... لَكَانَتْ: both the condition and result use كَانَ with لَوْ/لَـ. The result clause لَكَانَتْ سَعِيدَةً = she would have been happy. Note: سَعِيدَة in spoken form (without full tanwin).

cards.english: If you are angry, don't make decisions.
cards.word: إِذَا كُنْتَ غَاضِبًا لَا تَتَّخِذْ قَرَارَات.
cards.romanized: idhā kunta ghāḍiban lā tattakhidh qarārāt.
cards.grammarNote: Negative imperative: لَا + jussive (مجزوم). لَا تَتَّخِذْ = don't take/make (jussive of يَتَّخِذُ). Real condition with إِذَا followed by a negative command.

cards.english: If I were you, I would apologize.
cards.grammarNote: لَوْ كُنْتُ مَكَانَكَ (law kuntu makānaka) = if I were in your place. مَكَانَكَ = your place (accusative). This idiom is the standard Arabic equivalent of 'if I were you'.

cards.english: Whenever you want, I am here.
cards.grammarNote: كُلَّمَا (kullamā) = whenever/every time. Related to conditional expressions, it introduces a repeated condition. It is followed by the past tense and expresses repeated events: كُلَّمَا رَأَيْتُهُ ضَحِكَ (every time I saw him, he laughed).
Arabic doesn't simply add -s. Instead, many nouns change their internal vowel pattern to form the plural — these are called 'broken plurals.' The pattern must be memorized with each word.
كتاب → كتب. The long ā vowel disappears and the vowel pattern changes from kitāb to kutub. This is a broken plural — the shape of the word changes.
بيت (bayt) → بيوت (buyut). The vowel pattern shifts and a long u vowel is inserted.
رجل (rajul) → رجال (rijal). A long ā vowel is inserted. Many human nouns use this fa'al → fi'al pattern.
طفل (tifl) → أطفال (atfal). A prefix أ is added and vowels change — the أفعال pattern is one of the most common broken plural patterns.
صديق (sadiq) → أصدقاء (asdiqa'). Another أفعلاء pattern. Note the ء (hamza) at the end — common in broken plurals of this type.
Not all plurals are broken. Many words, especially loanwords and feminine nouns, take the 'sound' feminine plural by adding ات: سيارة → سيارات (cars), كلمة → كلمات (words).
كلمة (kalima) → كلمات. Add ات to the stem (drop the ة first): كلم + ات = كلمات. This is the sound feminine plural.
Masculine human nouns often take + ون (nominative) or + ين (accusative/genitive): مدرّس → مدرّسون (teachers). This is called the sound masculine plural.
مدرّس + ون = مدرّسون. Sound masculine plural — the word shape stays the same, only the suffix changes.
مدرّسة → مدرّسات. Drop the ة, add ات. Sound feminine plural.

The dual is formed by adding ـَانِ (-āni) in the nominative case. عَيْن (eye) → عَيْنَانِ (two eyes, nominative). In the genitive/accusative: عَيْنَيْنِ (-ayni). Arabic uses the dual for exactly two of anything.
يَد (yad) = hand. Dual: يَدَانِ (two hands, nominative) / يَدَيْنِ (genitive/accusative). Body parts that come in pairs naturally use the dual. When you say يَدَانِ you mean specifically two hands.

The definite dual adds الـ before the noun: الأُذُنَانِ = the two ears / both ears. The dual suffix ـَانِ remains. أُذُن (ear) is feminine, which affects adjective agreement: الأُذُنَانِ الْكَبِيرَتَانِ (the two big ears).
رِئَة (lung) is a feminine noun ending in ة (taa' marbuta). In the dual, the ة opens up to ت before the suffix: رِئَة + ـَانِ → الرِّئَتَانِ. This happens with all feminine nouns ending in ة.
After a preposition the dual takes the genitive/accusative form ـَيْنِ (-ayni): الْيَدَيْنِ (in both hands). كِلْتَا (kiltā) = both (feminine dual). For masculine: كِلَا (kilā).
عِنْدِي (ʿindī) = I have (lit. 'at me'). The dual subject عَيْنَانِ is in the nominative after عِنْدِي. Compare singular: عِنْدِي عَيْن = I have one eye.
وجع (waja') = pain, ache — very common in colloquial Arabic. Pattern to express pain: عندي وجع + body part (I have a [body part] ache).
عندي = I have (lit. 'at me'). رأس = head. عندي وجع رأس = I have head pain. This colloquial structure is used throughout the Arab world.
يؤلمني (yu'limuni) = hurts me, from the verb أَلَمَ (to hurt). This is the MSA structure: [body part] + يؤلمني. More formal than عندي وجع.
مريض (maridh) = sick (masculine). Feminine: مريضة (maridha). Colloquial alternative: أنا تعبان (ana ta'ban = I'm worn out / not feeling well).
مش = not (colloquial). بخير = well/fine. مش بخير = not fine/not well. Very natural in Levantine and Egyptian Arabic.
وين (ween) = where (Levantine). يوجعك = hurts you. MSA: أين يؤلمك؟ (ayna yu'limuka?).
هون = here (Levantine). MSA: يؤلمني هنا (yu'limuni huna).
حرارة (harara) = heat/fever. عندي حرارة = I have a fever (lit. 'I have heat'). Very common expression throughout Arabic-speaking countries.
بدي (biddi) = I want/need (Levantine). MSA: أحتاج طبيباً (ahtaj tabiban). دكتور is the common colloquial word for doctor.
كتير = a lot (Levantine). بوجعني كتير = it hurts me a lot.
يَجِبُ أَنْ (yajib an) = it is necessary that / must. The verb following أَنْ is in the subjunctive (المضارع المنصوب). The subjunctive of تَسْتَرِيحُ drops the final -u to give تَسْتَرِيحَ.

آخُذَ (ākhudha) is the subjunctive of آخُذُ (I take). Note the subjunctive ending -a instead of -u. دَوَاءً is indefinite accusative (tanwin -an). يَجِبُ is impersonal — it doesn't change for person/gender.

cards.english: You should go to the doctor.
cards.grammarNote: لَازِمٌ (lāzim) = necessary/must. It is common in spoken Arabic and MSA. Like يَجِبُ, it can be followed by أَنْ + subjunctive, or in colloquial usage directly by the present verb as shown here.
يَنَامَ is the subjunctive of يَنَامُ (he sleeps). The subjunctive is triggered by أَنْ after modal verbs. The verb agrees with its logical subject: يَنَامَ (he), تَنَامَ (she), أَنَامَ (I).
يَنْبَغِي (yanbaghī) = should/ought to — more formal than لَازِم. Negation: يَنْبَغِي أَلَّا (yanbaghī allā) = it should not that. أَلَّا = أَنْ + لَا contracted together.

cards.english: You must see the doctor immediately.

cards.grammarNote: مِنَ الضَّرُورِيّ أَنْ (min al-ḍarūriyy an) = it is necessary to. Another way to express strong obligation, slightly more formal. ضَرُورِيّ = necessary/essential.

cards.english: I must take the pills twice a day.
cards.word: يَجِبُ أَنْ آخُذَ الْحُبُوبَ مَرَّتَيْنِ فِي الْيَوْم.
cards.romanized: yajib an ākhudha l-ḥubūba marratayni fī l-yawm.
cards.grammarNote: مَرَّتَيْنِ (marratayni) = twice (lit. 'two times'), the dual of مَرَّة (marra = once). الْحُبُوبَ (al-ḥubūba) = the pills, accusative plural of حَبَّة (ḥabba = pill/grain).
